doc.title: Jerry Dodgion interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 9, 1996

chapter: Playing, influences and the Basie records
title: Grove Dictionary description and how he thinks about improvising
summary: Responding to the Grove quote, he says he never studied jazz formally, can't explain his playing, and that the best music happens when you let it.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I want to read something that was written about you in the Grove Dictionary of Jazz. See if you think that this guy knows what he’s talking about. He says: “Dodgion’s saxophone playing, influenced by that of Charlie Parker, Art Pepper and Jerome Richardson, is well represented by his inventive solo on ‘Tip Toe,’ which draws on blues formulas and demonstrates a relaxed rhythmic sense and the ability to develop motifs.”
Gee that’s pretty formal I guess.
Did you know you were a motif developer?
I never thought of it that way but it’s complimentary.
Yes, it is nice. When you play do you think about developing little lines and so forth or it just comes?

That’s hard you know because I never did really study how to play jazz. Like they have colleges that you can go to now and you can major in jazz. You can learn in three weeks now what took me fifteen years to learn. But I know it’s information-wise, you know? So it’s really hard, and I’m not a teacher either, I don’t do any teaching. So it’s hard for me to tell somebody how I feel about what I’m doing, it really is. So maybe if I were better at that I would have been a teacher. I don’t know.

Yeah. Well sometimes your own style is the hardest to talk about. I know I read about one fellow who did a very extensive study on Sonny Rollins and how he apparently developed all these motifs and after Sonny Rollins read it then he felt he couldn’t do it anymore, because now he was thinking too hard about it. Where before it was just a natural thing. Now that someone tells him what he’s doing, it’s hard to do now.

That’s possible. Because when you’re doing it, or when I’m doing it anyway, I’m not thinking of how I’m doing it. You just try to play your best and to fit in with what’s happening around you. That’s the main thing for me. I mean if I play with sensitive players it’s very easy to play and you don’t get tired, you have a lot of fun. And if you play with people that aren’t sensitive, that aren’t listening to each other and stuff, pretty soon you find, I’m really getting tired and the music is not fun, what am I doing here? I mean without getting too analytical about it, if it’s not fun and it’s not happening, you know it’s not happening. And just to keep playing and to try to make it happen is futile sometimes. Because when it’s really happening it’s not because you’re making it happen I don’t think. I think when it really happens is when you’re letting it happen. And that’s the best stuff. © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-
